catalog_quote: Summarizing up to this point, we have found stems (Classes A and B) with a HL melody, and those (Class D) with a HLHL melody. In general, before the application of rules of tone-simplification, all words in Tonga display tone melodies of the form (HL)... Tonga thus has what we called in Chapter 1 the factorization property, and tone-assignment may be viewed as an accentual process. We need only specify the association of a fixed tone in the tone melody to a lexically determined vowel in a given word. ... On this HL analysis, then, we find that the accent can fall on any vowel, and there can be two accents in a single morpheme, a perhaps surprising result. It should also be observed that the accent has no other local phonetic effects. In a recent phonetic study, Luce (1981) showed that there was no influence on length caused by the accent in Tonga. sweep_summary: Four sweep items, all about the tone/accent analysis of Zambian Tonga or a regional survey. Goldsmith 1984 (the catalog's deciding source) was re-read from the held author's scan and its pp. 22-23 statement confirms the TONAL coding verbatim (lexically placed tonal accent, no length or loudness correlate). Goldsmith 1983 (DOI 10.1515/9783112420065-014, De Gruyter, paywalled, bot-blocked landing) and Goldsmith 1981 (IULC mimeo, not found anywhere online) are the 8-page and draft precursors of the 1984 chapter by the same author; the author's site holds only related handouts ('Accent in Tonga: the Verbal System', 'Tone and Accent in Bantu'), viewed page by page, which are paradigms and rule schemata silent on phonetic stress; both precursors are low priority. Philippson 1991 (Paris 5 thesis, 542 pp) is a ~30-language East African Bantu tone/accent survey; theses.fr marks it not accessible online, HAL has no deposit, and the abstract does not say whether Tonga M64 is in its sample; medium priority as an overview only. Newly fetched sources to Goldsmith's page, Goldsmith 1987 BLS paper (Kintandu, not Tonga), the theses.fr and Crossref records; record in. No recode; best statement remains Goldsmith 1984.fr, archive.org and the author's site.

new_statements.citation: Goldsmith, John (1984). Tone and Accent in Tonga. In G. N. Clements & J. Goldsmith (eds.), Autosegmental Studies in Bantu Tone, pp. 19-52. Dordrecht: Foris. DOI 10.1515/9783110864465.19 (author's open scan, scanned locally).
new_statements.reading: Tonga is a two-tone Bantu language whose HL melodies are anchored to a lexically determined vowel ('accent'); that accent is a tonal device with no fixed position (any vowel, possibly two per morpheme) and no duration or loudness correlate. Coding TONAL stands. This is the catalog's existing deciding source re-read in this sweep, not a new source; nothing new was opened that states stress for Tonga.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. TONAL stands; the only competing statement in the saved material is Torrend 1891 sec. 302 n.1 (p. 61), a hedged 19th-century pan-Bantu 'light stress on the penult... generally less marked in Tonga than in Kafir', which is weaker and older than Goldsmith 1984 and is contradicted on the phonetic side by Hyman 2009 (Tonga: no length contrast, no penultimate lengthening).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding Goldsmith 1984 passage (scanned lines 170-216 = pp. 22-23) and the Fell 1918 p.10 secondary quote are verbatim in the held files, modulo trivial scanned normalizations; the catalog's display copy of the quote has a 'Classes reader and second reader' corruption ( correctly reads 'Classes A and B') that should be fixed cosmetically but does not affect the coding. (2) The record rests on a 1984 specialist phonology chapter that explicitly denies length and loudness correlates of the lexically placed tonal accent; the language is uncontroversially a two-tone Bantu system (Hyman 2017 p.165; Sibajene 2013 pp.38-39, fetched sources now). No reference grammar with a phonology chapter, JIPA illustration or instrumental prosody study newer than Carter 2002 was found in Glottolog (39 refs; the 'grammar' entries are pedagogical/missionary: Fell 1918, Torrend 1932, Hopgood 1940/19

sources.note: Tonga words carry (HL)-type melodies anchored by a lexically determined 'accent' (abstract tonal accent, lexically placed, can fall on any vowel, two per morpheme possible); the accent has no duration correlate (Luce 1981) and no perceptible loudness correlate. This is the catalog's own deciding source, re-read this sweep; identical wording (the catalog display string 'Classes reader and second reader' is a corruption of 'Classes A and B').

sources.citation: Sibajene, Alick (2013). A dialectological study of Tonga. MA dissertation, University of Zambia. xiii+140 pp. (UNZA DSpace hdl 123456789/3156)
sources.quote: 'These sound features are tone, length, stress and intonation. This section briefly highlights two prosodic features found in Tonga. These are tone and length.' ... 'Tonga is a tonal language ... Tonga realises two basic tones, high (H) and low (L).' p.39: contrastive vowel length (bowa 'mushrooms' vs boowa 'cowardice'). No stress rule anywhere in the thesis (grep: 'stress' only in a Greek-dialect example).

sources.quote: Lists a 'Tonga' among languages that 'have also lost the [PB vowel length] contrast but do not have PL [penultimate lengthening]' (table 27: Lexical contrast -, PL -). No Guthrie code given; since Zambian Tonga M64 retains contrastive vowel length (Sibajene 2013 p.39), this 'Tonga' is probably S62 or N15, so the statement cannot be safely attributed to tong1318.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.locator: theses.fr record 1992PA05H011: French and English abstracts; field 'accessible' = non
sources.note: Typological/diachronic survey of tone and accent across ~30 East African Bantu languages (from fully tonal Kikuyu to penultimate-demarcative-stress Swahili); the abstract names only Kikuyu and Swahili, so whether Zambian Tonga M64 is in the sample cannot be confirmed from the record. Full text is not online (theses.fr accessible=non; HAL lists 13 Philippson deposits, none this thesis; archive.org nothing). Any Tonga treatment would be a secondary synthesis of Carter/Meeussen/Goldsmith, so it would refine rather than overturn the coding.

Its existence and content are attested second-hand: Goldsmith's held handout 'Tone and Accent in Bantu' (p.1) lists 'Tonga (source: Carter 1962, 1971, 1972, Meeussen 1963, Goldsmith 1981, 1982)' and Goldsmith 1987 (BLS 13, p.88, fetched sources) describes his earlier Bantu papers as positing an 'accent' asterisk in the linear string from which tones are derived. It is the IULC draft of the same analysis published as Goldsmith 1984 and is superseded by it.
